doc.title: Victor Rendon interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, November 15, 2019 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Teaching by rote versus notating batá
summary: Oral tradition in Cuba, Rendón's own transcriptions and notation, and his Sunday class taught by rote.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: How do you teach what seems to be very complex rhythms and many rhythms. Where do you start with a novice?

Very good question. In Cuba it’s by rote. It’s an oral tradition and, I’ve been there, and what they do, and I’ve seen it happen here in the United States in New York City, the novice would basically sit there or maybe stand against the wall and just listen. They just pick it up by ear. And back in the old days they would do that for a couple of years or so, and if you were not an annoyance they would let you stay there and then maybe they would let you play and, like at a ceremony a lot of times the teacher will go to the beginner and he will play the drum this way so that he can follow him, or he will get behind him and tap you from your shoulder. I learned differently because being a percussionist that can read music I looked at transcriptions where I transcribed it myself

so I will actually write things out and then I’ll memorize it. But I find that looking at the paper reading it, it’s not the same because the sooner you can play it by memory then it becomes a part of you. Because for many years, like what you saw yesterday, I will read it like the newspaper. But it wasn’t until I put the papers away that I started to feel it spiritually within myself.
Would notated music for the batá have two staves? Would it be — because you’re playing two —
Yes, because the way I write it, there’s no standardized way. I write the left hand, I think — treble clef, I write the left hand on the E, the fifth space. And I write the right hand on the F space.
I’m thinking now, the right hand plays the lower tone, right?

Yes, yes, yes, yes. So A – E – A – E — F – E — F – E. And if I have like a muffled tone I’ll put it on the G space. But that’s my notation. It’s not necessarily standardized. Oh going back to the teaching, I do have a group of students coming in on Sundays and I’m teaching them by rote pretty much, even the ones that can read music. Once in a while I’ll take out a sheet of paper and I’ll show them, this is what it looks like. But for the most part my emphasis is that if you come in every week you’ll get it. You cannot go backwards, you can only go forwards you know.
